$comment: The mutation catalogue. Run it with `npx tsx scripts/mutate.ts`; docs/MUTATION.md explains why.
Each entry reintroduces a defect this project actually had, and names the test files that
claim to catch it. `find` must match its file EXACTLY ONCE -- the harness refuses to run
otherwise, because a mutation that did not apply looks exactly like a test that caught nothing.
The defects are historical, not invented: R129's audit took them out of git history, and the
test comments in src/ui/__tests__ say verbatim which mutation each guard was checked against.

mutations.claim: the runtime slider is a 44px target, not the user agent's ~15px default
mutations.note: Setting the height straight back to 15px passed 192 pins and 9 lobby cases before css.test.ts existed: everything guarding R118 was guarding the rule's NAME rather than its value.

mutations.claim: the thumb is drawn big enough to grab, not just boxed in something 44px tall
mutations.note: A 44px box around a default-sized thumb is a 44px box you cannot grab.

mutations.claim: the prefixed backdrop-filter is declared before the standard one, or the build ships only the prefix
mutations.note: Lightning CSS treats a later prefixed alias as superseding the standard property. Chrome supports only the standard one, so every frosted pane rendered flat -- in Chrome, in production, with dev and Safari fine and the @supports fallback correctly declining to fire.

mutations.claim: the failure panel names WHICH system did not answer
mutations.note: R129's 'assertion satisfied by its own neighbour': the middle third was toContain('Jellyfin'), a substring of the headline asserted one line above, so deleting this row left all nine cases green. Re-pointed when F3 moved the row's detail into the catalogue; the mutation still deletes the whole FROM row, which is the claim -- that the panel names WHICH system failed rather than leaving the host to read it as "the app is broken".

mutations.claim: the way out of a failure panel is wired to something, not just drawn
mutations.note: R129's 'control asserted and never pressed'. The panel explained a dead end and then was one; a button that does nothing puts it back.

mutations.claim: each vote button prints its word on the screen, not only in the DOM
mutations.note: R18/R26 forbid colour or symbol alone. The old assertion read container.textContent, which includes visually hidden text, so a glyph-only row passed (R129).

mutations.claim: nothing dims the vote weights, by any route
mutations.note: R129's 'one route checked where two exist': the guard forbade an opacity-70 CLASS, and dimming the identical pixels through an inline style sailed past it. -5 measured 2.82:1 on the screen a person reads fifty times an evening.

mutations.claim: pressing undo actually takes the vote back
mutations.note: Twelve cases named this row and its copy and none ever pressed it, so disconnecting the handler -- keeping the row, the label and the sentence verbatim -- left all twelve green (R129).

mutations.claim: the deck's cost line never promises the host approves the download first
mutations.find: text: 'Nothing is fetched from this screen.
mutations.replace: text: 'Your host approves it first. Nothing is fetched from this screen.
mutations.note: R129's 'negative pinned to one wording': the guard was the single literal /host is asked to approve/i, so the same false promise in other words shipped green. Matcher requests with an admin key and Jellyseerr auto-approves those by default, so no approval gate is a promise this app can keep. Re-anchored to the catalogue after R145/R146 moved the sentence there: a translation is now how this defect would be introduced, and it goes red in the catalogue AND in the rendered deck.

mutations.claim: the deck states no download size, because the app has none to state
mutations.find: text: 'Nothing is fetched from this screen.
mutations.replace: text: 'About 100 min of video. Nothing is fetched from this screen.
mutations.note: The old guard was /\d+\s?GB/i alone, which matches neither 'gigabytes' nor 'MB' nor R36's superseded 'About 100 min of video' -- the exact sentence R91 was written to kill, because 108 minutes is 2GB or 55GB depending on a release this app never sees. Re-anchored to the catalogue. The replacement is R36 superseded wording, which is what a translator with no context would plausibly reintroduce.

mutations.claim: peer progress on the deck is a count and never an identity
mutations.note: Ade cannot bear the room watching him be the slow one; R61 makes that a server promise rather than something the client declines to draw. Re-anchored to the catalogue: the peer count is now a template there, and a {who} placeholder is how naming would arrive.

mutations.claim: the genre wait announces itself, rather than being silent sr-only text
mutations.note: R129's 'reading the DOM where the claim is about the screen', inverted: the assertion read textContent, which cannot see an attribute, so deleting role="status" left the words in place and all eight cases green -- the exact state R85 was about, a screen reader meeting silence between 'I'm ready' and a list of genres.

mutations.claim: the elimination ballot's own header is a count, not a progress report about people
mutations.replace: <Bar left={`Waiting on ${members.filter((u) => u.id !== userId).map((u) => u.name).join(', ')}`} right={`${pool.length} left · 2 survive`} liveRight />
mutations.note: Two cases asserted the vote-out buttons exist and never looked at the bar above them, so turning the ballot's header into 'waiting on Bex' was invisible (R129). Re-anchored after R136 added liveRight to this line: the harness reported ERROR rather than KILLED, which is the distinction it exists to make -- an unapplied mutation looks exactly like a test that caught nothing. Re-anchored again after R145 moved the label into the catalogue: the harness reported ERROR rather than SURVIVED, which is the distinction it exists to make.

mutations.claim: signing in for Any Movie actually grants the scope the login was raised for
mutations.note: Deleting this made the neighbouring negative test STRICTER rather than red -- 'does not switch scope on a tap that needs an account' is satisfied by a lobby that never grants anything. A gate that never opens is not a gate.

mutations.claim: a tap that needs an account raises the gate instead of quietly changing the setting
mutations.replace: if (next === 'wide' && wideLocked) void updateSettings({ scope: next });
mutations.note: The first half of R111: the login that requirement raises used to reconnect the socket, which the server reads as the member leaving, so it deleted the seat that had just asked to sign in.

mutations.claim: the runtime row's title sits on the same step of the type scale as every other row
mutations.note: 0.875rem where every other row title is 1rem, in a grid with the identical gutter. A scale with one exception is not a scale.

mutations.claim: the slider carries the app's own styling rather than a bare accent colour
mutations.note: The shipped defect exactly: its only styling was a colour, so it took the user agent default and was the one control in the app that made the README's 'nothing you tap is under 44px' false.

mutations.claim: deck size is a real radio group, not three loose buttons
mutations.note: R129's 'fixture that renders one branch': this group renders only after DECK is tapped and no case ever tapped it, so stripping the role and every aria-checked passed. A cycle button makes a screen reader user tap through every option to discover what the options are.

mutations.claim: a phone with neither seat nor room reaches the join gate, not a spinner
mutations.note: R101's own fix sets BOTH to null (setUserId(null); setRoom(null)), so anything that lets the loading branch win leaves a refused rejoin on 'Loading room AB12' for ever. Swapping the two branches left all seven original cases green (R129); this is that defect in one line.

mutations.claim: a blocking failure gets THE screen, not a place on it beside the room
mutations.note: The old case asserted only that the headline appeared, so removing the !blocked guard -- drawing the failure AND the room at once, which is the state R98 is about -- left it green (R129).

mutations.claim: each room status draws its own screen and only its own
mutations.note: Every case in the file built its room with status KNOCKOUT, so LOBBY, SWIPING and FINISHED were never rendered: the auditor rotated three of the six branches to the wrong component and all seven cases passed (R129).

mutations.claim: dismissing the failure calls the thing that clears it
mutations.note: The server puts the room back to genre picking on a build failure; nothing ever cleared a diagnosis, so the room was recovered and every phone in the house was still stuck.

mutations.claim: the client waits longer than the server does before calling an action failed
mutations.note: 10s against the server's UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS of 15s: a slow Jellyseerr was reported to the phone as failed while the server was still working, and the retry that invited landed in Radarr as a second download. emitAck was never once invoked by this file.

mutations.claim: signing in updates socket.auth, so a later reconnect carries the token
mutations.note: R129's 'mock that discards the thing under test': io() returned a fresh literal per call and ignored its options, so this line could be deleted with all eight cases green.

mutations.claim: one socket for the life of the page
mutations.note: R111's failure mode by another route: without the guard every call constructs a fresh connection, and the server reads a teardown as the member leaving -- which is exactly how signing in used to destroy the seat it was signing in for.

mutations.claim: the ranking that explains a points winner survives a reload
mutations.note: R90 named five symptoms of a reload and the file reached four: no fixture ever set winnerRanking, so the group that explains WHY a film won on points was never rendered and dropping the fallback was invisible (R129).

mutations.claim: the winner screen never promises a host approval step on the branch where the server already accepted
mutations.find: text: 'Asked, and your server accepted it. It appears in Jellyfin once it finishes downloading.',
mutations.replace: text: 'Asked. It appears in Jellyfin once the host approves it.',
mutations.note: The old copy verbatim. Restoring it left nine of nine green, because /ada asked/i still matched (R129). There is nothing left to approve on this branch. Re-pointed at the catalogue when F3 moved the sentence out of WinnerScreen.tsx -- the claim is about what the room is told, and the catalogue is now where that is decided. The audit then caught a second, subtler error in that very re-point: the target file moved to strings.ts but `expect` still named winner.render.test.tsx, so the harness ran 14 cases that never look at this sentence and reported the claim hollow. Moving a mutation's FILE without moving the test that guards it is its own defect, and the only reason it was found is that a SURVIVED verdict is a gate failure rather than a note.

mutations.claim: the reject confirmation promises a return to the deck only when there is a deck to return to
mutations.note: The neighbouring case asserts the two labels on the TRIGGER and never presses it, so the confirm panel -- where R100's false promise lived -- was never mounted and reverting the copy inside it left nine of nine green. Re-pointed through F3's t() call; the ternary is the guarantee, not the literal.

mutations.claim: the abstain row can be spoken to: its accessible name contains the words on it
mutations.find: text: 'No preference — go with the room',
mutations.note: WCAG 2.2 A 2.5.3. The row reads "No preference" and was named "Abstain — go with the room", with not one word in common, so "click No preference" did nothing. It is the control R47 added FOR the person who does not want to invent an opinion, and it was the one a voice user could not reach. Moved to the catalogue by R145: the label now lives there and is used for BOTH the visible text and the accessible name, so that is where a translation would break it. It goes red in the catalogue AND in the rendered screen.

mutations.claim: the undo row can be spoken to: its accessible name opens with the words on it
mutations.find: ariaLabel={`Undo — ${behind.title}, puts the card back and clears your vote`}
mutations.note: WCAG 2.2 A 2.5.3. The row reads "Undo — <film>"; the name did not contain that phrase. The rule this is checked by walks every labelled control on four screens, so a third one is covered by existing rather than by somebody remembering.

mutations.claim: a text input is outlined by a token that clears 3:1, not a translucent white
mutations.note: WCAG 2.2 AA 1.4.11. A white overlay at 15% reaches 1.39:1 at BEST, composited over pure black; the real ground is lighter, so it is worse. That ring was the only thing marking a box you were meant to type in.

mutations.claim: the border token itself clears 3:1 against the ground
mutations.note: Moving the inputs onto the token is only worth anything while the token is bright enough. The test computes the ratio rather than trusting the name -- this mutation reports 1.46:1.

mutations.claim: the lobby ready count announces itself when somebody else presses ready
mutations.note: WCAG 2.2 AA 4.1.3. The lobby entire job: the number moves on everybody else phone with focus nowhere near it.

mutations.claim: the deck peer count announces itself
mutations.note: R46 makes this a bare count on purpose, and the count is exactly what the room IS allowed to know. It moved in silence.

mutations.claim: a viewport too short for the screen can still reach the vote controls
mutations.note: WCAG 2.2 AA 1.4.10. Measured at 320x256 (a 1280x1024 desktop at 400% zoom): the vote row ended at 372px on a surface that could not scroll, 116px out of reach. The first version of the guard was toContain(app-shell) over the whole file and this mutation PASSED it, because the comment above the element mentions the class.

mutations.claim: the home screen carries a typed name to the join gate
mutations.note: WCAG 2.2 A 3.3.7. Deleting this left the whole suite green before home.render.test.tsx existed: the CONSUMING half was covered in roomclient.render, the producing half nowhere. HomeActions was the only component in the app with no test of any kind.

mutations.claim: the join gate offers back the name the guest already gave
mutations.note: A guest has no account, so getAuthName() is null for exactly the person asked twice.

mutations.claim: a night appends what it learned instead of rewriting the whole ratings cache
mutations.note: U10 measured the old behaviour at 65 nights and 1.36 GB written to warm a 50,000-title library, because the request budget admits a few dozen titles a night while the write was the whole cache. Quadratic in the library.

mutations.claim: the library is fetched a page at a time, and the loop terminates on our terms
mutations.note: Removing this guard used to HANG the suite rather than fail it, because termination depended on the server being honest about TotalRecordCount. MAX_PAGES makes it fail cleanly at the ceiling instead -- a hang is a worse failure than a red test, and in a deck build it is the skeleton that never resolves.

mutations.claim: a server that ignores StartIndex and Limit cannot make the client collect the library once per page
mutations.note: A server is not obliged to honour paging. Without the dedupe the loop collected the whole library once per page up to MAX_PAGES -- fifty million objects at 50k titles, which died on a heap limit. Found because the performance benchmark stub ignores paging and was an adversary nobody designed.

mutations.claim: a translation cannot add the approval gate the app cannot enforce
mutations.find: text: 'Nothing is fetched from this screen.
mutations.replace: text: 'Your host approves it first. Nothing is fetched from this screen.
mutations.note: R107/R111 live entirely in wording. Once the sentence moves to a catalogue, a translator is the person most likely to undo them, and they cannot see the ruling from the string.

mutations.claim: the peer count template can interpolate numbers and nothing else
mutations.note: R46/R61: peer progress is a count and never a name. A placeholder called who would be the whole defect arriving through the back door of a translation file.

mutations.claim: a catalogued sentence is not also hardcoded in a component
mutations.replace: detail="Nothing is fetched from this screen. If it wins, someone still has to ask — and whether that starts a download straight away depends on your Jellyseerr settings."
mutations.note: Two copies of a load-bearing sentence is worse than the one it started as: the rendering tests assert the SCREEN, so the component copy is what ships and the catalogue copy is what a translator edits. They drift silently. This was the actual state after the knockout migration.

mutations.claim: a restored room brings its seat secrets, or nobody can rejoin it
mutations.note: R86 checks a rejoin against the seat secret, so a restore without them hands back a room every member is a stranger to. The restore would LOOK like it worked and every phone would be told "That seat is not yours to take" -- which is what this mutation actually prints.

mutations.claim: a night the idle TTL already reaped does not come back
mutations.note: A room from three days ago must not return because the server happened to restart. Same TTL the sweeper uses, so the two cannot disagree.

mutations.claim: everybody comes back disconnected until they prove otherwise
mutations.find: for (const user of Object.values(room.users)) user.connected = false;
mutations.note: Their sockets died with the process. A member marked connected with no socket behind them is the stall R112 is about: connectedness is the sole test of who can hold a room up, so a ghost makes the room wait for somebody who cannot answer.

mutations.claim: the deck-finished wait is a count and never names anybody
mutations.replace: Waiting for {others.map((u) => u.name).join(', ')} to finish — then the points decide.
mutations.note: R46/R61. Shipped for months because the naming test rendered the NOT-done state and the done-state test asserted two phrases that could not see a name -- R129 shape, a fixture that renders one branch. Found by a focus-group persona reading the screen he stares at while the evening stalls, not by the audit.

mutations.claim: no waiting state on any screen names a peer
mutations.note: R46/R61 as a RULE rather than the one instance R151 fixed. The deck broke it for months because its own R46 test rendered the not-done state; this renders every waiting state on every screen that has one. The lobby is the single deliberate exception (R44: the host must know who is in the room before reading the code aloud).

mutations.claim: a stale socket cannot evict somebody from a room that came back from disk
mutations.note: R149 made this worth pinning. `seatSockets` is deliberately not snapshotted -- every id in it names a connection that died with the process -- so a restore leaves it empty, and `ownsSeat` answers TRUE for an unknown seat by design. R112 survives only because `disconnect` reads its identity from the socket's own session data, which only a successful join sets, and both join paths claimSeat in the same breath. That coupling is what this mutation defends: break it and every restored room loses the protection silently.

mutations.claim: a component keeping its own copy of a short catalogued word is still caught
mutations.note: The duplication guard was `code.includes(text)`, which is right for a sentence and meaningless for a word: "No" is inside "Nothing" and "Not your fault". That made every short word uncatalogueable -- and No, Yes and Maybe are exactly what a translator changes. R154 made the short case look for the string as it would actually be WRITTEN. This mutation is the proof the sharpening did not cost the guard its teeth: restore the component's own copy of a two-character word and it still goes red.

mutations.claim: every screen a room spends its evening on has one first-level heading
mutations.note: F8 in docs/ACCESSIBILITY.md: the deck rendered SwipeCard's film title as an <h2> with no <h1> above it anywhere on the page, so heading navigation landed on a film claiming to be a second-level heading under nothing. The heading is sr-only, which is exactly why a person cannot notice it going missing -- nothing on screen changes. Only a test that mounts the screen and counts can.

mutations.claim: a catalogued sentence renders its element where the placeholder is
mutations.note: Dropping the slot leaves the sentence's own words intact and only the product name or the server address missing -- 'We use  for requests.' A guard asserting the surrounding copy would not notice, which is why the tests assert the element IS markup and that an unfilled slot stays visible.

mutations.claim: a sentence written inline with its tag is caught, not just one on its own line
mutations.note: R159 shipped with a stated blind spot: its whole-line rule could not see a sentence inline with its tag, and Reconnecting... had to be found by hand. Requiring a closing tag right after the text closes it without reintroducing the collision that made the first attempt unusable -- useState<string>(x) has no </ after it. This mutation is the proof the second rule bites where the first could not.
